journal_name: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

abstracts.abstract: The increasing heterogeneity in modern computing systems necessitates a fundamental rethinking of how instruction-level parallelism (ILP) and thread-level parallelism (TLP) interact. This paper introduces the Multi-dimensional Parallelism Coordination Theory (MPCT), a novel theoretical framework that formalizes the interdependencies between ILP and TLP in heterogeneous architectures. Unlike traditional approaches that treat these parallelism dimensions as orthogonal optimization targets, MPCT establishes a unified cost model capturing the trade-offs among computational resources, memory bandwidth, and energy consumption. The framework introduces key concepts including parallelism elasticity, resource contention coefficients, and dynamic balancing invariants. We rigorously prove that optimal parallelism configuration in heterogeneous systems follows a convex optimization landscape, enabling efficient search algorithms. Evaluations conducted on diverse GPU architectures and CPU-GPU heterogeneous systems demonstrate that MPCT-based optimization achieves 1.3-1.8x performance improvement over state-of-the-art approaches while reducing energy consumption by 25-40%. This paradigm shift provides architects and compiler designers with a principled foundation for navigating the complex design space of modern parallel architectures.

Accurate performance prediction is crucial for architectural design space exploration and system optimization, yet existing models inadequately capture the complex interactions within deep memory hierarchies of modern processors. This paper presents the Hierarchical-Aware Performance Model (HAPM), which significantly advances performance modeling by incorporating fine-grained memory bandwidth contention dynamics across cache levels. The key improvement over prior work lies in our analytical formulation of inter-core cache interference under varied thread-level parallelism configurations. HAPM introduces cache contention factors that dynamically adapt based on workload characteristics and memory access patterns, enabling precise prediction of performance degradation in congested scenarios. We validate the model through extensive experimentation on contemporary multi-core processors with varying cache hierarchies. Results demonstrate that HAPM reduces prediction error from 15-25% (achievable with conventional models) to merely 5-8%, while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for early design-stage exploration. This improved accuracy directly benefits architects in making informed decisions about memory hierarchy design and workload scheduling strategies.

GPU architectures face fundamental challenges in efficiently handling irregular workloads with divergent memory access patterns, resulting in severe performance degradation and energy inefficiency. This paper introduces GPULP, a Load-aware Programmable Register Allocation Framework that fundamentally reimagines register file management through software-hardware co-design. GPULP comprises three novel components: (1) a compiler-level workload analyzer that classifies memory access patterns and predicts register pressure, (2) a hardware substrate with dynamically reconfigurable register allocation units supporting adaptive spill code generation, and (3) a runtime scheduler that coordinates between warp scheduling and register allocation to minimize memory traffic. Unlike conventional fixed register file organizations, GPULP enables fine-grained control over register allocation decisions at instruction granularity. Implementation on a cycle-accurate GPU simulator demonstrates that GPULP achieves 1.4x average speedup for irregular workloads from the Rodinia and SHOC benchmarks while reducing energy consumption by 32% compared to state-of-the-art register allocation strategies. This paradigm establishes a new design point for future GPU architectures targeting diverse application domains.

Data prefetching remains a critical technique for mitigating memory latency, yet conventional hardware prefetchers struggle with complex access patterns exhibited by modern workloads. This paper presents AdaptPref, an Adaptive Neural-Enhanced Memory Prefetcher that substantially improves prefetch accuracy through learned pattern recognition. AdaptPref employs a hybrid architecture combining a lightweight LSTM network for temporal pattern extraction with a decision tree for spatial correlation modeling, enabling accurate prediction across diverse memory access behaviors. The system features an online learning mechanism that continuously adapts to phase changes and program evolution without requiring offline training. We implement AdaptPref as a last-level cache side-channel prefetcher with negligible area overhead (less than 2% of cache area). Evaluation using SPEC CPU 2017 and PARSEC benchmark suites shows that AdaptPref achieves 28% and 35% performance improvement respectively, with 18% reduction in memory subsystem energy consumption compared to state-of-the-art prefetchers including BINGO and SPP. The design demonstrates that neural-enhanced prefetching is practical for real-world deployment while maintaining low latency and power budgets.
